# **Architectural Redesign and Implementation of the Q-MINI IncusOS Hybrid Ternary-Binary Framework**

The demand for localized, high-throughput artificial intelligence inference and quantum-inspired cryptography has exposed the fundamental thermodynamic and architectural limitations of traditional Base-2 (binary) von Neumann computing architectures. To transcend these hardware boundaries, the Q-MINI IncusOS framework introduces a paradigm shift in operating system design by partitioning computational workloads based entirely on their fundamental mathematical logic base.1 This hybrid environment seamlessly integrates a Native Galois Field 3 (GF3) ternary underlay with a standardized Base-2 binary overlay, orchestrated via an immutable root filesystem and a high-performance system container manager.1

The impending rewrite of the q\_mini\_wasm\_v2 infrastructure necessitates a rigorous evaluation of the hardware abstraction layers, memory packing algorithms, asynchronous initialization lifecycles, and zero-latency inter-process communication (IPC) bridges that make this architecture viable.1 The analysis indicates that successfully migrating from theoretical ternary models to production-ready edge deployments requires deep integration with advanced silicon, specifically leveraging spatial compute arrays rather than traditional arithmetic logic units (ALUs).1 This report provides an exhaustive, peer-level architectural blueprint for rewriting and deploying the Q-MINI IncusOS framework, addressing hardware compilation, kernel-level driver isolation, immutable image generation, and topological routing algorithms.

## **Hardware Abstraction and Spatial Compute Acceleration**

The foundation of the Q-MINI IncusOS framework relies entirely on the underlying silicon's ability to natively accelerate non-binary logic. Standard x86\_64 central processing units evaluate data strictly in base-2, making the emulation of ternary logic computationally atrocious and thermodynamically inefficient.1 To achieve native GF3 execution—where states are represented as ![][image1]—the architecture abstracts the system's Neural Processing Unit (NPU) away from standard machine learning inference tasks, repurposing it as a dedicated quantum-logic coprocessor.1

The primary hardware target for this deployment is the AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, internally codenamed "Strix Halo".1 This system-on-a-chip (SoC) represents a massive leap in unified memory architecture and spatial compute density, boasting a total silicon footprint of 441.72 square millimeters that integrates advanced CPU, GPU, and AI acceleration capabilities within a single package.5 The architecture centers on two 67.07 square millimeter CPU Core Complex Dies (CCDs) and a substantial 307.58 square millimeter I/O die.5

| Component Specification | Architectural Details | Q-MINI Framework Operational Role |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Central Processing Unit | 16 "Zen 5" Cores, 32 Threads, up to 5.1 GHz Boost, 80 MB Total Cache (16 MB L2 \+ 64 MB L3), 45-120W cTDP 6 | Reserved strictly for traditional Base-2 floating-point workloads executing within the unprivileged Incus overlay containers.1 |
| Graphics Processing Unit | RDNA 3.5 Architecture, Radeon 8060S, 40 Compute Units, up to 2900 MHz 4 | Handles legacy floating-point video rendering, DSP audio engines, and standard spatial visualizations.1 |
| Neural Processing Unit | XDNA 2 Architecture, Up to 50 INT8 TOPS (Total Platform TOPS up to 126\) 6 | Repurposed to natively accelerate GF3 matrix operations, tropical geometry routing, and ternary cryptography. |
| Unified Memory Subsystem | 256-bit LPDDR5X-8000 interface, 256 GB/s bandwidth, Up to 128 GB Total Capacity 5 | Enables zero-copy memory semantics between the CPU's binary space and the NPU's ternary execution space.4 |

The AMD XDNA 2 NPU architecture abandons the traditional von Neumann bottleneck in favor of a spatial dataflow design.11 It consists of a two-dimensional array of compute and memory tiles built with AI Engine technology.3 A single row of memory tiles creates a pool of software-managed on-chip L2 memory, allowing the compute tiles to process data in parallel with deterministic data movement via dedicated Direct Memory Access (DMA) engines.3 For the Q-MINI framework, this spatial arrangement is critical. The framework utilizes the SYCL backend—specifically implemented in the sycl/tableau\_kernels.cpp and message\_passing\_sycl.cpp source files—to map GF3 ternary operations directly onto these hardware tiles.1

By offloading Galois Field 3 operations to the NPU via the Linux kernel, the system bypasses the CPU's binary ALUs entirely.1 The spatial partition is established by programming the column isolation registers via the NPU's internal microcontroller, creating concurrent, hardware-protected host access utilizing Process Address Space IDs (PASIDs).3 This allows the q\_mini\_wasm\_v2 core to execute intent-based AI telemetry, advanced quantum-inspired cryptography (such as Gottesman-Knill bit-ledger verification), and topological Betti number extraction securely at Ring 0, operating at an extreme thermodynamic energy target of less than 1 picojoule per operation (![][image2]).1

## **Kernel Drivers and Hardware Isolation**

To bridge the operating system with the physical spatial arrays of the Strix Halo APU, the framework relies heavily on the amdxdna Linux kernel module, which is part of the broader Linux accelerator (accel) subsystem.1 The driver is responsible for managing the multi-user AI inference hardware and provisioning the necessary execution contexts.3

The boot flow of the native GF3 underlay requires the amdxdna driver to use the Platform Security Processor (PSP) to securely load the signed NPU firmware and kick off the boot sequence of the NPU microcontroller.3 The driver then waits for a specific alive signal in a designated location on Base Address Register 0 (BAR 0).3 The microcontroller runs firmware responsible for command processing, array partition setup, and workload orchestration.3 The NPU firmware uses a dedicated instance of an isolated non-privileged context called the Execution Ring (ERT) to service each workload context and execute user-provided control code.3 Simultaneously, it uses a single isolated privileged context called MERT to service management commands originating directly from the amdxdna driver.3

To successfully compile the custom Linux kernel required for the Q-MINI IncusOS image, developers must ensure that the kernel configuration explicitly enables AMD IOMMU Shared Virtual Addressing (SVA) and the accelerator subsystems. The kernel compilation flags must include CONFIG\_DRM\_ACCEL=y and CONFIG\_AMDXDNA=m.1 Furthermore, because the NPU requires substantial memory allocation to function as a GF3 coprocessor, the underlying operating system must have memory locks explicitly unbounded in the security configurations (e.g., configuring \* soft memlock unlimited and \* hard memlock unlimited within the /etc/security/limits.d/ directory).15

## **The Immutable Underlay: Systemd and mkosi Integration**

To ensure the deterministic integrity of the ternary logic plane, the Q-MINI IncusOS does not function as a traditional, mutable Linux distribution. Instead, it relies on an immutable root filesystem generated via the mkosi (Make Operating System Image) utility.1 The underlay forms the highly privileged intelligence layer of the system, running the Incus daemon and the Q-MINI execution engine exclusively at the kernel and near-kernel levels.1

The build pipeline leverages the mkosi.conf configuration standard to declare a reproducible, locked operating system tree.17 This provides deep integration with modern systemd features, including UEFI Secure Boot, Unified Kernel Images (UKI), and Trusted Platform Module (TPM 2.0) measurements for robust full disk encryption.17 The mkosi tool operates as an advanced wrapper around distribution package managers (such as apt or dnf), resolving dependencies and constructing the file system in a highly customized, reproducible manner.16

The strategic choice to utilize an immutable underlay stems directly from the requirement to execute sensitive cryptographic workloads natively in GF3 without the risk of interception.1 If the underlay were mutable, malicious or misconfigured user-space applications could introduce binary pollution, compromising the mathematical security of the quantum-inspired states. Consequently, atomic A/B partition updates are employed, ensuring that any failed system update gracefully rolls back to a known-good ternary state using distinct block devices.1

Injecting the q\_mini\_wasm\_v2 runtime into this mathematically locked environment requires specific, non-standard modifications to the image build tree. The framework utilizes the mkosi.extra/ directory protocol.1 During the image assembly phase, mkosi natively overlays the contents of the mkosi.extra/ directory onto the root filesystem immediately after the base distribution packages are installed, but before the image is finalized, converted to a read-only SquashFS or raw Btrfs structure, and cryptographically signed.17

| Target Image Path (via mkosi.extra/) | Component Description | Operational Role in the OS |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| /opt/qmini/bin/qmini-gateway | Go WebAssembly / IPC Bridge Binary 1 | Binds to the host Unix socket, listens for incoming Base-2 payloads from the overlay, and dispatches them via CGO. |
| /opt/qmini/lib/libq\_mini\_wasm\_v2\_core.so | C++ GF3 SYCL Runtime Library 1 | The core compiled execution engine that interfaces with the amdxdna driver to execute tensor computations on the XDNA 2 NPU hardware. |
| /etc/systemd/system/qmini-underlay.service | Systemd Daemon Unit Configuration 1 | Initializes the Q-MINI gateway automatically at boot, ensuring strict process ordering and NPU permission mapping. |

To guarantee hardware access without compromising the zero-trust architecture, the qmini-underlay.service unit is strictly configured. The daemon must be initialized only after the NPU driver is loaded, dictated by the After=network.target amdxdna.service directive.1 Furthermore, the service executes the Go gateway (ExecStart=/opt/qmini/bin/qmini-gateway \--socket=/run/qmini/host-api.sock) while binding the process to the render group.1 This group assignment is critical, as udev rules managed by the kernel explicitly restrict read and write permissions for /dev/accel/accel0 to the render group, effectively shielding the NPU from unauthorized access by standard background services.1

## **Overlay Orchestration and Zero-Latency IPC Bridging**

While the native GF3 underlay manages quantum-inspired cryptographic algorithms, AI telemetry, and the WebAssembly runtime, standard enterprise edge operations still inherently require traditional floating-point mathematics and standard Linux networking protocols.1 The Q-MINI framework satisfies this dual-requirement through the deployment of a Binary Base-2 Overlay, orchestrated exclusively by Incus.1

Incus, acting as the system container and virtual machine manager, provides secure Linux Containers (LXC) namespaces and Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) environments.1 Workloads such as container-vyos (which handles standard Border Gateway Protocol and EVPN network routing) and vm-madvr (which executes heavy floating-point video rendering tasks) operate inside this overlay.1 Because these instances execute on the traditional AMD Zen 5 CPU cores, they process strictly in base-2 and are entirely isolated from, and unaware of, the underlying ternary fabric.1

The most formidable engineering challenge in this hybrid design is facilitating instantaneous, high-throughput communication between the binary containers in the overlay and the ternary intelligence running in the underlay.1 Traditional container networking approaches, which rely on virtual bridged interfaces (such as incusbr0) and standard TCP/IP traversal, introduce unacceptable protocol stack latencies, contextual switching overhead, and serialization costs.1

To circumvent the TCP/IP stack entirely, the framework implements a Zero-Latency Unix Socket Inter-Process Communication (IPC) Bridge.1 The Q-MINI Go Gateway—running persistently on the underlay—binds to a high-performance Unix Domain Socket at /run/qmini/host-api.sock.1 The Incus daemon is then explicitly configured to inject this host socket directly into the isolated, unprivileged containers via an Incus proxy device.1

While a standard proxy deployment in Incus allows for cross-protocol mapping (e.g., forwarding host TCP traffic to a container Unix socket), the zero-latency requirement demands a strict unix \<-\> unix configuration utilizing non-NAT mode.23 Network Address Translation (NAT) mode is restricted strictly to TCP and UDP proxying and inherently alters packet flow, making it incompatible with raw socket byte streaming.23 The custom Incus profile automatically applies the proxy device configuration to all dependent overlay instances:

| Incus Proxy Parameter | Assigned Value | Functional Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| type | proxy | Defines the device as a traffic forwarding mechanism.23 |
| bind | instance | Instructs the proxy to create the listening socket *inside* the container namespace, rather than on the host.1 |
| listen | unix:/var/run/qmini/api.sock | The virtual socket path created inside the Base-2 container where the application writes its payloads.1 |
| connect | unix:/run/qmini/host-api.sock | The destination socket on the GF3 underlay where the Go Gateway actively listens.1 |
| mode | 0666 | Sets open read/write file permissions on the listening socket within the container.1 |
| security.uid / security.gid | 1000 / 1000 | Drops privileges to the standard unprivileged container user, ensuring the proxy process does not execute as root.1 |

When an application inside the binary overlay needs to query the artificial intelligence or verify a state—for example, the VyOS router attempting to verify a secure BGP cryptographic ledger—it simply writes a binary JSON or Protobuf payload directly to its local virtual socket (/var/run/qmini/api.sock).1 The Incus proxy seamlessly streams this data to the host. The qmini-gateway receives the payload, translates the request via CGO bindings into the C++ SYCL core, evaluates the state natively in GF3 on the Ryzen NPU, and streams the ternary result back through the socket.1 This structural design creates a unified execution environment where the binary networking plane and the ternary intelligence plane act as a single, cohesive entity with microsecond response times.1

## **Algorithmic Breakthroughs: Tropical Geometry and Stabilizer Simulation**

The reliance on GF3 ternary states is not merely an exercise in memory packing; it enables profound algorithmic optimizations in tensor calculus, specifically by addressing the thermodynamic energy costs associated with Large Language Model (LLM) routing and quantum simulations.1 The architecture adopts the principles of the BitNet b1.58 specification, restricting neural network synaptic weights strictly to the set ![][image3].

This single hardware-enforced modification eliminates floating-point matrix multiplications entirely. In traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) neural networks, the expert routing mechanism relies heavily on Softmax attention gates, which require energy-intensive, floating-point Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units.2 The Q-MINI SYCL backend discards Softmax entirely in favor of Tropical Geometry—specifically, operations over a max-plus semiring.

In the max-plus algebra simulated within the message\_passing\_sycl.cpp kernels, standard arithmetic is replaced to bypass the MAC units natively. Tropical Addition is mathematically redefined as the Maximum operation, while Tropical Multiplication is mapped directly to GF3 Modulo Addition over the symmetric set ![][image3]. By replacing complex matrix multiplications with simplified integer addition trees, the system calculates shortest-path geometric affinities for expert routing natively on the NPU.

Furthermore, the system leverages GF3 Gaussian elimination to extract Quantum Betti Numbers, defining topological feature structures natively.1 Topological features in the telemetry data are grouped elegantly using balanced ternary properties: a state of ![][image4] identifies a Verified Persistent Feature, a state of ![][image5] indicates a Superposition or Boundary Phase, and a state of ![][image6] flags a Destructive Artifact or noise boundary.2

Finally, the framework supports local qutrit entanglement simulations. Rather than computing exponentially large density matrices typical of quantum emulation, the engine utilizes a Ternary Symplectic Pauli Frame (TSPF) paired with Stabilizer Tableaus.1 Controlled-NOT (CNOT) operations are resolved through simple GF3 tracking; if a Pauli collision occurs during state evaluation, the phase offset is inverted mathematically without complex linear algebra, maintaining the strict sub-picojoule energy target.1

## **WebAssembly Memory Architecture and Ternary Packing**

While the underlying NPU hardware accelerates GF3 operations natively, the primary high-level execution target for the application layer is WebAssembly (WASM).2 WebAssembly is fundamentally a strict 32-bit (and progressively 64-bit) binary execution environment that evaluates instructions using binary opcodes and manipulates data within a purely linear, byte-addressed memory space.2 The inherent friction between a binary virtual machine and the native ternary mathematics of the underlay necessitates a high-speed mathematical virtualization layer.2

Storing a single ternary digit (trit) within an 8-bit memory byte wastes approximately 80% of the allocated memory footprint and destroys L1 cache locality during high-throughput tensor operations.2 To maximize radix economy and eliminate binary pollution, the q\_mini\_wasm\_v2 architecture deploys two distinct bit-packing algorithms depending on the memory bus and register target: the TritPack5 structure for byte-aligned storage, and an escalating 20-trit schema for WASM 32-bit linear memory integers.1

### **The TritPack5 Schema**

For granular data structures, such as zero-allocation tokenization dictionaries and Key-Value (KV) cache compression layers, the framework packs exactly 5 trits into a standard 8-bit byte (uint8\_t).1 Mathematically, 5 trits yield ![][image7] discrete states.1 Because an 8-bit byte holds exactly 256 physical states, storing 5 trits consumes approximately 95% of the byte's absolute capacity, achieving an information-theoretic entropy efficiency of 99.06%.1 This dense alignment minimizes memory bandwidth saturation, allowing a 100-edge topological complex to be compressed into a mere 20 physical bytes.1

### **The 20-Trit Escalating Accumulator**

When operating directly on the active execution stack inside the WASM sandbox, optimizing for 32-bit integer (i32) throughput becomes paramount.2 The absolute maximum numeric value of an unsigned 32-bit integer is ![][image8], which equates to ![][image9].2 The largest integer power of 3 that can be stored continuously without triggering an arithmetic overflow within this strict 32-bit boundary is ![][image10], which evaluates to ![][image11].2

Consequently, mathematical law dictates that exactly 20 distinct balanced trits (![][image1]) can be efficiently embedded into a single i32 block.2 Given an array of 20 unbalanced trits denoted as ![][image12], where each element ![][image13], the final packed 32-bit WASM integer ![][image14] is accumulated via the following polynomial evaluation:

Note: In the physical implementation, a fixed offset is applied to the balanced trits to map them to positive integers ![][image16] prior to bitwise shifting. This 2-bit per trit encoding (00=0, 01=1, 10=-1) prevents signed integer bleed during low-level logical hardware serialization.2

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Bit Allocation per State | 8.0 bits (1 byte) | \~1.58 bits | Extreme Density |

When the WASM execution instance fetches this packed block from its linear memory stack to perform operations—such as Betti number extractions or Clifford sum gates—it executes a highly optimized unwrapping loop. The engine utilizes successive binary division and modulo operators (Value / 3 and Value % 3), optimized directly by the host's WebAssembly compiler, to aggressively reconstitute the 20 discrete trits back onto the execution stack where the virtualized ternary opcodes can process them.2 This architecture offers an overall 27% reduction in physical storage footprint compared to uncompressed 8-bit arrays of the same numerical range 2, a critical optimization given the memory-bound cascade failures previously identified in the MoE routing modules.1

## **Asynchronous Data Ingestion and Lifecycle Management**

The programmatic conversion of massive academic research telemetry and legacy datasets—which inherently originate in floating-point Base-2 formats—into the dense 20-trit WASM linear memory is a highly intensive, CPU-bound operation.2 If this Base-2 to Base-3 conversion pipeline is executed synchronously within the WASM environment, the heavy division-remainder mathematics threaten to block the main execution thread, stalling the entire application layer and rendering the interface unresponsive.2

To definitively mitigate this architectural bottleneck, the framework enforces a rigid asynchronous execution lifecycle prior to WASM initialization.2 Drawing deep structural inspiration from Python ASGI lifecycle management tools like asgi-lifespan (maintained by a network of contributors including @kennetholsenatm-gif), the Q-MINI framework dictates a discrete "Startup/Initialization Phase" that isolates the heavy translation logic outside the boundaries of the active WASM engine.2

The data ingestion lifecycle is orchestrated across four strictly defined stages:

1. **Staging (The Cold Buffer Entry):** Raw binary packets, such as high-frequency network flow states or classical machine learning weights, are ingested into a lock-free, circular NVMe buffer via the IngestAPI.2 The payload is timestamped, assigned a unique Correlation ID, and tagged with a TERNARY\_READY: FALSE metadata flag.2 This decouples the high-frequency volatile data streams from the computationally expensive conversion engine.2  
2. **Parallel Transformation (The Trit-Mapper):** A pool of highly concurrent asynchronous worker threads pulls the 32-bit binary segments from the buffer.2 The floating-point values are normalized to fixed-point integer scales, and the recursive division-remainder algorithm transforms the classical values into balanced ternary arrays.2  
3. **Validation and Checksumming (The Integrity State):** Before the 20-trit arrays are fully packed and committed, a ternary parity check is executed.2 The sum of the trits within the block is calculated and compared against an appended parity bit (Trit 19 in the packed word).2 If the validation fails due to data corruption, a Single-Bit Flip Recovery (SBFR) algorithm is attempted; if recovery is mathematically impossible, the block is ejected to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for retry.2  
4. **WASM Injection and Persistence (The Sink):** Only after the dataset is fully translated and validated is the qminiwasm-core WASM instance fully initialized.2 Its internal linear memory stack is pre-allocated, and the 32-bit packed integers are streamed directly into memory utilizing SharedArrayBuffer structures.2 The lifecycle uses Atomics.notify and Atomics.wait to efficiently signal the WASM engine that the ternary batch is ready for computation.2 The original binary buffer is then cleared, and a callback is issued.2

This strict separation of concerns allows the underlying AMD CPU hardware to sustain throughputs exceeding 1.2 million conversions per second per core, achieving average latencies of less than 50 microseconds from ingestion to final packing, all while ensuring the WASM runtime remains completely unblocked for immediate topological analysis.2

## **Strategic Implementation and Future Mitigation**

Deploying this highly sophisticated architecture from theoretical conceptualization to bare-metal production requires a meticulously phased orchestration plan. Current telemetry indicates that the system faces potential "memory-bound cascade failures" when the tropical MoE routing algorithms attempt to scale beyond the L2 cache constraints of the NPU.1

### **Phase I: Substrate Hardening and mkosi Stabilization**

The immediate priority involves locking the mkosi build pipeline and stabilizing the amdxdna driver interactions to prevent race conditions during boot.1 Ensuring that the Ryzen AI NPU's spatial compute arrays are securely exposed to the qmini-gateway daemon at Ring 0, while keeping the rest of the OS immutable, is the foundational milestone.1 Extensive validation of the A/B atomic partition schema must be conducted to guarantee that kernel panics induced by early SYCL memory leaks trigger automatic, failsafe rollbacks without corrupting the cryptographic ledgers.1

### **Phase II: IPC Optimization and Container Migration**

With the native GF3 underlay stable, the secondary objective focuses on the Incus orchestrator.1 The deployment of the zero-latency Unix socket bridge will be benchmarked under high load. Pilot programs involving the migration of non-critical Base-2 development workloads (such as simple routing daemons) into the binary overlay will be tested to analyze IPC bottlenecks.1 Current projections indicate that massive, high-throughput Base-2 video workloads (e.g., vm-madvr) may saturate the Unix socket serialization buffer, increasing latency.1 To permanently mitigate this, future revisions of the Incus configuration will target direct memory access (DMA) allocations and shared memory mapping into the containers, bypassing Unix socket serialization overhead entirely for heavy payload handoffs.1

### **Phase III: Ecosystem Expansion and WASM SDK**

The final phase centers on expanding the broader WebAssembly ecosystem.1 As the 20-trit packing algorithms and TritPack5 structures become mathematically standardized, the native WASM SDK will be deployed to third-party developers.1 This will allow edge devices and browser-based clients to stream massive ternary datasets directly into their execution environments, bypassing standard binary pollution.2 The completion of this phase will establish the Q-MINI IncusOS framework not merely as a specialized edge operating system, but as a fully scalable, hybrid architecture capable of bringing quantum-inspired efficiency to off-the-shelf, low-power hardware.
